generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: The lightweight Civic tuners still hunt for. Double-wishbone suspension at both ends and VTEC engines made it handle and rev like cars costing twice as much.

generations.name: Tenth generation
generations.note: Turbocharging went range-wide, and the Civic Type R finally came to America, 306 hp, front-wheel drive, and a Nürburgring record to answer the doubters.

generations.name: Eleventh generation
generations.note: Quieter, more grown-up styling, same formula underneath. The Type R makes 315 hp and remains manual-only, which is exactly the point.

models.intro: Started as a fuel-crisis runabout and grew into the compact benchmark. Every generation has had a version worth caring about, and the Type R versions are among the best front-drive cars ever made.

generations.name: Seventh generation (North America)
generations.note: Peak simple Accord: a smooth 3.0L V6, an available six-speed manual coupe, and build quality that explains why so many are still running.

generations.name: Tenth generation
generations.note: The V6 died and nobody mourned for long, the 2.0T borrowed from the Civic Type R's family tree made this the quickest Accord yet.

generations.name: Eleventh generation
generations.note: Hybrid powertrains take over the upper trims, styling goes subtle, and the manual is gone. Efficient and refined, if less playful than before.

models.intro: The family sedan for people who actually read reviews. The Accord spent decades trading best-in-class wins with the Camry, and usually won on steering and feel rather than on price.

models.collectorNote: First-generation cars are the collectible ones, manuals over automatics, documented timing-belt service over low miles alone. Second-gen cars are still depreciating into interesting territory.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: All-aluminium body and engine, titanium connecting rods, and a VTEC V6 that revved to 8,000 rpm. Later 3.2L cars made 290 hp. It made mid-engine cars usable every day.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: Twin-turbo V6 plus three electric motors and torque-vectoring all-wheel drive. Very fast and very clever; the Type S finale lifted output to 600 hp.

models.intro: The supercar that embarrassed Ferrari on reliability and usability, then came back 25 years later as a hybrid. Ayrton Senna helped develop the first one. That fact alone tells you the intent.

models.collectorNote: Values punish modifications and reward paperwork. A stock AP1 with full history is worth more than a faster one with a story.

generations.name: First series
generations.note: The purest version: 2.0 litres, 9,000 rpm redline, and handling that rewarded commitment and punished sloppiness. No traction control. You were the traction control.

generations.name: Second series (North America)
generations.note: A stroked 2.2L engine traded 800 rpm of redline for usable torque, and the chassis was softened slightly. The Club Racer (CR) of 2008 is the collector pick.

models.intro: A 9,000 rpm love letter to the naturally aspirated engine. The F20C made 120 hp per litre, a record for a production road car at launch, and the shifter is still the benchmark every manual is judged against.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: A Civic underneath, a picnic table hidden in the cargo floor, and a side-hinged tailgate with the spare on it. Charming in a way modern crossovers rarely try to be.

generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: Turbo power arrived, the interior got genuinely good, and Honda Sensing safety tech went standard on most trims. The one most used buyers should target.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: Bigger, boxier, and hybrid-led at the top of the range. The Sport Touring Hybrid is the one Honda expects most buyers to pick, and it's right.

models.intro: One of the original car-based crossovers, and still the sensible default in the segment. It has never been exciting. It has also never really been beaten at the job it was built for.
